title: Why Evaluation Is the Hard Part
summary: An agent's output is open-ended and nondeterministic: the same input can produce different text every run, and text that 'looks good' is often subtly wrong. You cannot ship, improve, or trust an agent you cannot measure, so evaluation — not the model — becomes the hard, central engineering problem. A good eval loop is the flywheel that turns changes into reliable progress instead of guesswork.
nestedConcepts: you can't ship what you can't measure

subtopics.title: Agent outputs are open-ended, not one right answer
subtopics.explanation: Traditional software has an exact expected output you can diff against; an agent can phrase a correct answer a hundred ways, and many tasks (summaries, plans, code) have no single canonical string. This means you can't assert `output == expected` and be done. Evaluation is hard precisely because correctness lives in the meaning, not the exact characters, which is what pushes teams toward semantic and rubric-based scoring.
subtopics.example:
expected = "The capital of France is Paris."

# all of these are 'correct' but none equal `expected`
candidates = [
    "Paris is the capital of France.",
    "It's Paris.",
    "The French capital is Paris (pop. ~2.1M).",
]

# naive check fails on every valid answer
for c in candidates:
    print(c == expected)   # False, False, False
# exact-match is useless here -> you need semantic evaluation

subtopics.title: Nondeterminism: same input, different output
subtopics.explanation: LLMs sample from a probability distribution, so temperature, model version, and even provider load can change the output run to run. A test that passes once may fail the next time for reasons unrelated to your change. Because a single run tells you almost nothing, evaluation has to run many cases and reason about rates, not one-off results.

subtopics.title: 'Looks good' is not the same as correct
subtopics.explanation: LLMs are optimized to be fluent and confident, so wrong answers read just as smoothly as right ones — a hallucinated citation or a plausible-but-false number sails past a quick eyeball check. Skimming a few outputs and nodding is the most common way teams fool themselves. Real evaluation checks claims against ground truth, which is why you build labeled datasets instead of trusting vibes.
subtopics.example:
answer = (
    "According to a 2019 Stanford study, 87% of users "
    "prefer dark mode."
)

# reads as authoritative -> but is it true?
cited_study_exists = check_source("2019 Stanford dark mode 87%")
print(cited_study_exists)   # False: the study was hallucinated
# fluent != factual; you must verify against ground truth

subtopics.title: You can't ship what you can't measure
subtopics.explanation: Without a number, every prompt tweak or model swap is a coin flip: you have no way to know if a change helped, hurt, or did nothing, and no way to catch a regression before users do. 'It felt better in the demo' does not survive contact with production traffic. A measurable score is the gate that lets you deploy changes with confidence instead of hope.
subtopics.example:
# before: no eval -> shipping on vibes
deploy(new_prompt)   # did it get better? nobody knows

# after: a score gates the change
baseline = evaluate(old_prompt)   # 0.82 pass rate
candidate = evaluate(new_prompt)  # 0.79 pass rate
if candidate >= baseline:
    deploy(new_prompt)
else:
    print("regression: 0.82 -> 0.79, do NOT ship")
# measurement turns guessing into a decision

subtopics.title: Evaluation is the flywheel
subtopics.explanation: Once you can measure quality, every part of development accelerates: failures point you to gaps, fixes are validated by the score, and new edge cases get folded back into the dataset so the same bug can't return. Each turn of the loop makes the agent better and the eval set stronger. This compounding cycle — measure, diagnose, fix, re-measure — is why teams that invest in evals out-iterate teams that don't.
subtopics.example:
def flywheel(agent, eval_set):
    while True:
        results = evaluate(agent, eval_set)   # 1. measure
        failures = [r for r in results if not r.passed]
        gap = diagnose(failures)              # 2. diagnose
        agent = improve(agent, gap)           # 3. fix
        eval_set += new_cases_from(failures)  # 4. grow the set
        # 5. loop -> each turn compounds quality

foundations.overview: Building an agent is the easy part; knowing whether it actually works is the hard part. Unlike deterministic software, an agent produces open-ended, nondeterministic text: the same prompt yields different wording each run, correct answers take many forms, and wrong answers are just as fluent as right ones. That combination defeats exact-match tests and human eyeballing alike. Evaluation is the discipline of measuring quality rigorously — over many cases, against ground truth, with numbers you can compare. It's what lets you catch regressions, justify a model swap, and ship with confidence instead of vibes. Crucially, evaluation isn't a one-time gate but a flywheel: measure, find failures, fix them, fold the new cases back into your dataset, and re-measure. Teams that build this loop early out-iterate everyone else, which is why 'the hard part' of agents is almost always the eval, not the model.
foundations.formalDefinition: Agent evaluation is the systematic measurement of an agent's behavior against defined success criteria across a representative set of inputs, producing comparable scores that account for the open-endedness and nondeterminism of LLM output, used to detect regressions and drive iterative improvement.
foundations.whyItMatters: Every decision you make about an agent — ship it, tune the prompt, swap the model, add a tool — is only as good as your ability to tell whether it helped. Without measurement you fly blind, regressions reach users silently, and 'improvements' are indistinguishable from noise. Evaluation converts an unpredictable text generator into an engineering artifact you can reason about, which is the prerequisite for trusting it in production.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of an agent like a new hire whose work you can't grade with an answer key, because there's no single right answer and they do the task slightly differently each time. You can't judge them on one polished-looking memo. Instead you give them a rubric and a stack of representative tasks, score their work over the whole stack, and keep adding the tasks they got wrong to next week's set. Evaluation is that rubric-plus-task-stack, run continuously.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Deciding whether GPT-5 actually beats your current model on your workload; catching a prompt change that quietly dropped answer quality; proving to stakeholders an agent is safe to launch; regression-gating every pull request that touches the agent; and prioritizing which failure mode to fix next based on where the score is lowest.
commonUseCases: Gating deploys and PRs on a measured quality score
Comparing models or prompts objectively before a swap
Catching silent regressions before users do
Prioritizing fixes by where the agent scores worst

commonMisconceptions.myth: If the demo looks good, the agent is good.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Demos cherry-pick easy inputs and one lucky run. Fluent output hides wrong facts, and nondeterminism means the next run may differ — only measurement over many representative cases tells you the truth.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Exact-match testing works like it does for normal code.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Correct answers take many forms, so `output == expected` fails on valid outputs. Agent eval needs semantic, rubric-based, or ground-truth checks, not string equality.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Evaluation is a one-time step before launch.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It's a continuous flywheel. New failures become new test cases, and you re-measure on every change; a static, stale eval set stops catching the regressions that matter.

interactiveWidget.title: The eval flywheel in one picture
interactiveWidget.caption: Evaluation isn't a gate you pass once — it's a loop. Each failure you find becomes a new test case, so the same bug can never come back, and every change is validated by a number instead of a hunch.

config.note:
Measure -> Diagnose -> Fix -> Grow the set -> Re-measure.

Start: run your agent over a labeled eval set and get a score (e.g. 82% pass).

1) MEASURE: the score is your ground truth, not the demo.
2) DIAGNOSE: look only at the failures — they point straight at the gaps.
3) FIX: change the prompt / tool / model to address that gap.
4) GROW: add every new failure as a permanent test case so it can't regress.
5) RE-MEASURE: did the score go up? Ship only if it did.

The magic is compounding: each turn makes both the agent AND the eval set stronger. Teams with a tight flywheel out-iterate teams shipping on vibes, because they can tell signal from noise. 'Looks good' is a feeling; a rising score is evidence.

checkpoints.prompt: Why does exact-match testing (`output == expected`) fail for most agent tasks?
options: String comparison is too slow at scale
Correct answers can be phrased many different ways, so valid outputs don't match the one expected string
The model always adds trailing whitespace
Exact match only works for numbers
checkpoints.explanation: Agent outputs are open-ended: 'Paris is the capital' and 'It's Paris' are both correct but neither equals a single expected string. Correctness lives in meaning, so you need semantic or rubric-based scoring, not string equality.

checkpoints.prompt: An agent runs the same prompt 3 times at temperature 0.7 and you assert the output equals a fixed string. What's the most likely result across runs?
checkpoints.code:
expected = "Your daily grind, perfected."
for _ in range(3):
    out = run_agent("Give me a coffee slogan", temperature=0.7)
    print(out == expected)
options: Mostly False — nondeterministic sampling produces different wording each run
True on the first run only, guaranteed
checkpoints.explanation: At non-zero temperature the model samples different completions each call, so a fixed-string assertion is flaky and mostly False. One run proves nothing — you measure rates over many cases instead of asserting a single exact output.

checkpoints.prompt: You tweak the agent's prompt and it 'feels better' in a quick demo. Why is that not enough to ship?
options: Demos are always slower than production
A demo is a cherry-picked input on one lucky, fluent run — it can hide wrong facts and won't reveal a regression on real traffic
You must always A/B test with real users first
Prompts can't be changed after launch
checkpoints.explanation: Fluent output hides errors, and one run under nondeterminism means nothing. Only a measured score over a representative set tells you whether the change actually helped or introduced a silent regression.

keyTakeaways: Agent outputs are open-ended and nondeterministic, so exact-match tests and single runs can't tell you if they're correct.
Fluent, confident output ('looks good') routinely hides wrong facts — verify against ground truth, don't trust vibes.
You can't ship, tune, or trust an agent you can't measure; a score turns every change from a guess into a decision.
Evaluation is the hard, central problem of agent engineering — usually harder than building the agent itself.
Treat eval as a flywheel: measure, diagnose failures, fix, fold new cases back in, and re-measure so quality compounds.
